entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during thunderstorms that lasts a few seconds and then vanishes, with or without leaving traces. No accepted explanation exists, and most evidence is eyewitness accounts.
entries.background: Reports go back centuries, but the phenomenon has rarely been recorded by instruments. Many theories exist and none is accepted.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist who wrote Sur le tonnerre (1837), where the term ball lightning took hold. He also received Lorenzo Butti's letter about the 1841 Milan sighting.

entries.name: Lorenzo Butti
entries.background: Marine painter at the Austrian imperial court who saw a fireball in Milan in June 1841 and wrote about it to Arago.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: School official who wrote Der Kugelblitz (1923), the only German-language monograph on ball lightning. He collected many old reports, including Arago's.

entries.name: Rakov and Uman handbook
entries.background: Standard reference book on lightning by Vladimir Rakov and Martin Uman (2003). Its chapter 20 reviews ball lightning.

entries.name: Stenhoff
entries.background: Mark Stenhoff's 1999 book on ball lightning, with about 2400 references. It is the main English-language compilation of cases and theories.

entries.name: Stanley Singer
entries.background: Author of the 1971 book The Nature of Ball Lightning, an early broad compilation of reports and theories.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Russian physicist who keeps a database of ball lightning reports, including accounts by scientists.

entries.name: Fragmented science
entries.background: Phrase coined by Turner in 2001 for ball lightning research, which is done by scattered individuals with little coordination.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: Austria's network of sensors that records the time, place and strength of lightning strikes.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: Germany's lightning location network, run by Siemens.

entries.name: positive stroke
entries.background: A lightning strike carrying positive electric charge to the ground. Positive strokes are far rarer than negative ones, typically about a tenth of strikes, but are often stronger.

entries.name: Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa
entries.background: Soviet physicist and Nobel laureate who proposed a theory of ball lightning.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist and a member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna. He sketched and reported a ball lightning seen in Vienna in 1868.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at Göttingen. As a child he saw ball lightning split into smaller spheres that melted road asphalt.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: Yale palaeontologist, famed for dinosaur discoveries, and president of the US National Academy of Sciences.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German experimental physicist known for the 1922 Stern–Gerlach experiment, which showed that the spin of atoms takes only certain fixed values in a magnetic field.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer and later physics professor at the University of Kent. His 1963 in-flight sighting of a glowing sphere passing down an airliner aisle became widely known.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Physicist at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, killed by electricity in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.background: Temporary paralysis, numbness or loss of feeling after a lightning strike, which usually clears within hours.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician, founder of modern neurology, at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris. He taught Sigmund Freud, who translated his lectures into German.

entries.name: Dorstone
entries.background: A 1936 report from Herefordshire, England, of a red-hot ball that fell into a tub of water and made it boil. It is often used to estimate how much energy ball lightning holds.

entries.name: Rozlyn Krjcik
entries.background: New York woman who saw a blue sphere at her front door in 2008. Her glass porch window was later tested for radiation-induced fluorescence.

entries.name: Camp Blanding experiment
entries.background: A 2008 experiment in Florida in which rocket-triggered lightning was aimed at over 100 ground materials. It produced glowing effects but the researchers did not call them ball lightning.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.background: A 2012 recording on the Qinghai Plateau in China in which cameras with a diffraction grating captured the light spectrum of a ball lightning. The spectrum showed iron, calcium, silicon, nitrogen and oxygen lines.

entries.name: Mitino incident
entries.background: A 2015 Moscow case in which three people filmed a glowing object with mobile phones. Triangulating the videos gave its height and speed.
